finding.claim: The DELETE /reports/:id handler calls the async authorize() without await. The returned promise rejects with the 403 error, but nothing waits for it, so execution continues straight to db.reports.remove() and the report is deleted without any authorization check. The rejected promise is never handled. On Node 15 and later it causes an unhandledRejection, which by default crashes the process. That gives an attacker a denial of service on top of the bypass.
finding.source: Any request from a user who has no 'delete' grant on the report. This also covers a user with no session, because req.user would be undefined and authorize would reject with a TypeError, which is equally ignored. The attacker controls the :id path parameter.
finding.sink: db.reports.remove(report.id) at server.js:21, which permanently deletes the report.

trace.note: The report is loaded by the attacker-supplied req.params.id
authorize(...) is called without await, so the returned promise is dropped and any rejection is ignored
The grants check runs asynchronously and throws a 403 error, but only inside the dropped promise
db.reports.remove runs unconditionally and deletes the report
The handler returns 204 to the attacker

finding.guards_checked: Compared with the PUT handler at line 27, which does await authorize. No auth middleware, try/catch, or express error wrapper protects the DELETE route. The middleware at line 4 only copies the session user and enforces nothing. The authorize() check itself is correct but never gates the operation. No ownership check or second guard exists before the removal.

verdict.guard_found: authorize() at server.js:9-16 throws a 403 on missing grants, but the DELETE handler at line 20 calls it without await, so the rejection is dropped. The middleware at server.js:4-7 enforces nothing. There is no try/catch and no other check.
verdict.reason: server.js:20 calls the async authorize() as a bare statement, so its 403 rejection (thrown at server.js:14) never gates db.reports.remove at server.js:21; the awaited call at server.js:27 shows the intended pattern, and any low-privilege or sessionless user can trigger the delete.

verdict_facts.guard_found: none effective: authorize() at server.js:9-16 throws on failure, but the DELETE handler at line 20 calls it without await, so the rejection never stops line 21. The middleware at lines 4-7 only copies the session user. There is no try/catch and no ownership check.
verdict_facts.reason: server.js:20 calls async authorize() as a bare statement, so its 403 rejection (lines 11-14) is dropped and db.reports.remove at line 21 runs for any caller, unlike the PUT handler, which awaits at line 27.

finding.claim: Mass assignment: PUT /reports/:id passes the entire request body to db.reports.update with no field allow-list. A user with only 'write' grant can overwrite fields they should not control, such as owner, id, or other protected fields. Whether this is exploitable depends on the db.reports.update implementation, which is not in this codebase. Plausible rather than confirmed.
finding.source: The JSON body of PUT /reports/:id, which is fully attacker-controlled.

trace.note: The write grant is checked, but only for the report id and not for which fields are changed
The raw req.body is passed to update

finding.guards_checked: The authorize 'write' check at line 27 is awaited correctly. There is no schema validation, field allow-list, or immutable-field protection. The db layer is not present, so any protection inside update could not be checked.

verdict.guard_found: authorize(user,"write",report) at server.js:27 is awaited and throws on missing grant, so only users with a write grant on that report reach the update. It does not restrict which fields are written. There is no allow-list, schema validation or immutable-field check in server.js.
verdict.reason: server.js:28 passes raw req.body to db.reports.update, and the trace lines are accurate. The authorized attacker needs only a write grant. Whether protected fields such as owner or id can be overwritten depends on db.reports.update, which is not in the repo (server.js is the only file), so exploitability cannot be decided.

verdict_facts.guard_found: authorize(user, "write", report) at server.js:27 is properly awaited and throws 403 on failure; no field allow-list or schema validation on req.body
verdict_facts.reason: Trace is accurate: server.js:3 parses the body and :28 passes raw req.body to db.reports.update after the awaited write check at :27. Exploitability depends on the db.reports.update implementation, which isn't in this directory (only server.js exists). The attacker is an authenticated user with a write grant, who may legitimately edit the report but not necessarily its owner or id.
